svg.aria-label: Diagram: Conditional Access session controls and report-only mode on Microsoft Entra, showing the default 90 day rolling sign-in frequency window, why require reauthentication every time is bounded by five minutes of clock skew, the four report-only result states and which of them means a control was never exercised, and the resilience defaults behaviour during an outage including the conditions the backup authentication service cannot evaluate in real time
svg.title: The grant is the easy half: the session that follows it, and proving a policy works before it does
svg.text: Access was granted. Now the session — and whether you can prove any of it first.
Part two of #41a. Session controls shape what happens after the decision; report-only is the only way to see a policy work before it does.
Sign-in frequency: the default is 90 days, and Microsoft argues against shortening it
“The Microsoft Entra ID default configuration for user sign-in frequency is a rolling window of 90 days.” The stated reasoning:
“Users who habitually enter credentials without thinking might unintentionally provide them to malicious prompts.”
“Don’t ask users to provide their credentials if the security posture of their sessions hasn’t changed.”
A short frequency is a security control on paper and a phishing-training exercise in practice. The posture change is what revokes.
“Every time” does not mean every time
“The policy factors in five minutes of clock skew when every time is selected, so that it doesn’t prompt users more often than
once every five minutes.” And it fires “when the session is evaluated” — so “if the user closes and opens their browser during
the session lifetime, they might not be prompted for reauthentication”. Without MFA it “might result in sign-in looping”.
Report-only: four results, and only two of them tested anything
Success
conditions and non-interactive controls were all satisfied
Failure
conditions matched, a control was not satisfied — a real result
User action required
the control was never exercised. “The user isn’t prompted to satisfy
the required controls.” MFA and terms of use land here.
Not applied
the conditions did not match — says nothing about the controls
Resilience defaults: the trap is the blast radius
On by default. During an outage the Backup Authentication
Service reissues tokens for existing sessions — which are
“more than 90% of authentications to Microsoft Entra ID”.
“Disabling resilience defaults for a policy that applies to a
group or role reduces resilience for all users in the tenant”
— including users the policy never applied to.
Cannot be evaluated live in an outage: group membership,
role membership, sign-in risk, user risk, country/region,
and authentication strengths.
What you cannot test at all
“You can’t conduct a dry run using the Backup Authentication
Service or simulate the result of a policy with resilience
defaults enabled or disabled.”
“Conditional Access doesn’t support classical A/B testing.”
And report-only is not invisible: a report-only policy that
checks device compliance “can prompt users on macOS, iOS,
and Android devices to select a device certificate”, and
“these prompts can repeat until the device is compliant”.
Exclude those platforms from report-only compliance checks.
The session control nobody reads until an audit
A persistent browser session leaves cookies on the device after it closes, and those “might access Microsoft Entra artifacts, which
remain usable until token expiration, regardless of the Conditional Access policies applied to the resource environment. So, token
caching can be in direct violation of desired security policies for authentication.” The convenience and the control are the same
setting pointed in opposite directions — and during an outage, sessions are extended even where sign-in frequency says otherwise.
Sources: Session controls, Adaptive session lifetime policies, Conditional Access policy insights and report-only mode, and Resilience defaults, on Microsoft Learn.
